# Changelog

All notable changes to this project are documented here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/), and the project aims to
adhere to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

Entries are not edited here by hand. Each change adds a small file under
`changelog.d/`; at release time `scripts/assemble-changelog.mjs` rolls the
pending fragments into a new version section below the marker.

## Unreleased

## [1.1.0] - 2026-08-15

### Added

- `check-failure-notifier-coverage --require-alert-priority`: a workflow step
  invoking a local composite action that declares an OPTIONAL `priority:` input
  must pass one. Omitting it is not neutral — the call site silently inherits the
  urgency the action chose, which for an alert action is the maximum, and a repo
  whose every alert arrives at max urgency has trained its owner to swipe them
  all away, so the one that mattered is the one that gets ignored. The trigger is
  the invoked action's own declared inputs, never an action name, so a house
  alert composite is covered the day it grows a defaulted `priority`. Cosmetic
  inputs (`tags:`) are deliberately not required: priority is what drives phone
  behaviour, and demanding every optional input would make this noise rather than
  a severity discipline.
- `check-argument-exit-swallow` (Tier 1 · Honesty): flags a command substitution passed as an ARGUMENT — `my_helper "$(risky_listing)"` — in a file that runs under `set -e`. The shell discards the substitution's exit status, so `set -e` reports on the outer command, which succeeds on empty output. This is the sibling of shellcheck's SC2155 (`local x="$(cmd)"`) one syntactic step over, and shellcheck has no rule for it. The check fires only when the outer command is a function that the scanned file, or a file it sources, defines: `echo "$(date)"` and `grep -q "$(f)" file` are idiomatic and are the bulk of the matches, and a call to a function this tree owns is the shape where the author meant the failure to propagate. A source path the shell computes (`source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib.sh"`) resolves by its trailing literal name against the tracked shell files. Everything else is a node shape on the bash grammar (`_bash_ast`), so a substitution in a `variable_assignment`, in a `command_name`, in a printed message, or in a heredoc body is out of scope. Opt out with a reason-bearing `# allow-argument-exit: <reason>`. Included in the `check-tier1` aggregate.
- Automated release-readiness path adapted from `agent-glovebox`: a daily
  scheduled workflow (`release-readiness.yaml`) asks Claude whether the pending
  `changelog.d/` fragments merit a release and, on a yes, opens a
  `release`-labelled PR that bumps `package.json` and rolls the `CHANGELOG` on an
  `auto-release/vX.Y.Z` branch. A human merges it; `tag-release.yaml` then tags
  `vX.Y.Z`. It never pushes to the default branch, so it needs no ruleset-bypass
  credential. It opens the PR with the organization PAT, because this
  organization refuses a pull request that `GITHUB_TOKEN` opens.
  Complements the human `release`-label path in
  `release-prep.yaml` and stands down when any `release` PR is already open so the
  two never collide. A self-managed tracking issue
  (`manage-release-failure-issue.sh`) surfaces a broken scheduled run.
- `check-bare-return-status` (Tier 2): a bare `return` or `exit` hands back the status of the last command that ran, so the `&&` or `||` in front of it decides the value. `A && return` is always 0, and a `||` after a test is always 1. The check requires an explicit `return 0` / `return 1` where the forwarded status is a constant. It never flags `cmd || return`, which forwards the command's own code (127, 42). Opt out with `# allow-bare-return: <reason>`.
- `check-cancellable-required-check` (Tier 2, opt-in): flags a workflow that declares a required check (`# required-check: true` marker) AND carries a **static** (ref-less) workflow-level `concurrency.group` with a truthy `cancel-in-progress`. A sibling ref then cancels the running job — and its workflow-level `always()` reporter — wholesale, so the reporter never posts and the required check hangs at "Expected — Waiting" forever. This is the residual class the static-concurrency lint misses: it keys off the explicit required-check marker, catching marker-based required checks that have no decide-gate heuristic. Per-ref groups and non-cancellable groups pass. Opt out with `# cancellable-required-check-ok`.
- `check-case-default` (Extras): requires a bare `*)` default arm on every shell `case … esac` block so an unexpected value runs something instead of silently leaving variables unset. Opt out with `# case-default-ok: <reason>` on the `case` line.
- `check-claude-model` (Extras, opt-in): flags any `anthropics/claude-code-action` step that omits an explicit model (`--model` in `claude_args`, or a `model:` input), which silently bills the action's default Opus tier. Opt out per step with `# allow-default-model` on the `uses:` line.
- `check-cron-alert-coverage` (Extras): fails a scheduled workflow whose failures reach nobody — a cron has no PR surface, so its red is visible only to whoever opens the Actions tab. Fails closed: every scheduled workflow must route its failures to a human, by a notification step a failure can reach (`if: failure()`, `needs.x.result != 'success'`), by a failure notifier in the tree listing its `name:` in `on.workflow_run.workflows`, or by a reasoned `# cron-alert: false  # <reason>` marker. A repo that deliberately routes its crons nowhere passes `--allow-unrouted`, which narrows the check to the two lies rather than muting it: a malformed marker, and a notification step behind a success-only gate (`if: success()`, `needs.x.result == 'success'`) that reads as coverage but fires never. `--notifier-pattern REGEX` (repeatable) extends the built-in notifier patterns rather than replacing them.
- `check-cron-comment` (Extras): fails a workflow schedule whose comment cadence claim (hourly/daily/weekly/monthly/every N …) contradicts the cron expression's shape; ambiguous crons and claim-free comments always pass. Opt out with `# cron-comment-ok`.
- `check-echo-fallback` (Tier 2): flags `|| echo`/`|| printf` fallbacks that convert a failure into a benign parseable string, inside command substitutions and as unaborted bare statements; stderr-redirected or aborting recoveries pass. Opt out with `# echo-fallback-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-env-symmetry` (Extras): scans the whole tracked tree for every env var matching a `--prefix` and flags any that is written but never read (or read but never written) — the half-finished-rename signature where the reader silently sees an unset value. Conservative extraction keeps false positives near zero; dynamically-composed names are skipped, and an out-of-band var opts out with `# env-symmetry-ok: <VARNAME> <reason>`. Needs `args: [--prefix, <PREFIX>]`; not part of a tier aggregate.
- `check-externalized-markers` (Tier 2, opt-in): flags any workflow job where a policy marker (default: the git history-rewrite commands `git commit --amend` / `git rebase` / `git filter-branch` / force-pushes) is reachable only through `bash .github/scripts/*.sh` or `uses: ./.github/actions/*` indirection, never in an inline `run:`. That delta is the exact blind spot of a guard that scans only inline `run:` text — such a guard passes vacuously once the command is externalized. Markers match whole command tokens (so `git push --force` doesn't fire inside `git push --force-with-lease`). Add repo-specific markers with `--marker '<cmd>'`; opt a step out with `# allow-externalized-marker: <reason>` on the invoking `run:` or in the referenced script.
- New Tier 2 hook `check-failure-notifier-coverage`: round-trip freshness check keeping `ci-failure-notify.yaml`'s `on.workflow_run.workflows` list equal to the tree's set of push/schedule-triggered workflow names (`workflow_run` has no wildcard, so the list is a derived copy). Prints the corrected YAML block on mismatch, flags monitored workflows missing a `name:`, and passes silently when the notifier is absent unless `--require-notifier` is set.
- New `check-folded-scalar-comment` (Tier 1, honesty): flags a line written as a
  `#` comment inside a folded (`>` / `>-`) YAML block scalar. A folded scalar has
  no comment syntax, so the line is folded into the **value** — and when that
  value is an argument string something shell-splits, the `#` opens a shell
  comment and every argument after it is discarded. The failure shape is the
  worst available: the file documents a boundary that is not in force. Scoped to
  a folded block that also carries a `-`-leading line (an argument string, not
  prose), which is what keeps it quiet on `run:` bodies and Markdown; literal
  (`|`) scalars keep newlines and are deliberately out of scope. Opt out with
  `# allow-folded-scalar-comment: <reason>`.
- `check-frozen-head-sha` (Tier 1, honesty): flags any workflow or composite-action step whose `run:` script or a `with:` input value references `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`. That SHA is frozen at trigger time, so a force-push or an autofix `--amend` after the trigger makes it point at a diverged commit — a diff-range step then silently mis-scopes to the whole branch, and a checkout lands a stale tree. Derive the head from the checkout (`git rev-parse HEAD`) instead. `base.sha`/`head.ref` never match. Opt a genuine lease-pinning use out with `# frozen-head-ok: <reason>` in the step's source block; `env:`-routed uses are out of scope.
- New `check-gh-slurp-jq` (Tier 1, honesty): flags a `gh api` call `gh` refuses
  to run — `--slurp` alongside `--jq`/`--template`, or `--slurp` with no
  `--paginate`. Both are rejected while `gh` parses its arguments, before any
  request goes out (verified against gh 2.86.0, with valid-flag controls proving
  the rejection precedes the HTTP request), so the call exits non-zero on _every_
  run: it has never worked. That is worse than a loud bug — a site that swallows
  the failure reads as a permanent green, and one that does not reds a scheduled
  job 100% of the time. Backslash-continued calls are read whole, so a `--jq` on
  a later line still counts, and flag matching is confined to the pipeline
  segment the `gh api` token opens so a downstream `| jq -r …` is never mistaken
  for one of its flags. Opt out with `# allow-gh-slurp-jq: <reason>`.
- `check-job-timeout` (Tier 2): requires every GitHub Actions job to declare `timeout-minutes` instead of inheriting GitHub's 360-minute (6h) default, so one wedged step can't pin a shared runner slot for six hours. Reusable-workflow (`uses:`) jobs are exempt; opt out with `# allow-no-timeout: <reason>`.
- `check-lockstep-pins` (Tier 2, standalone): config-driven twin-pin equality — each `--pair FILE1 REGEX1 FILE2 REGEX2` must extract exactly one value per file and the values must match; zero/multiple matches is a hard error. Not in the `check-tier2` aggregate.
- `check-multi-cron-gating` (Extras): fails a workflow that declares two or more distinct crons whose jobs cannot tell one cron from another. GitHub starts every schedule-eligible job on EVERY cron fire, so a job gated on the bare `github.event_name == 'schedule'` runs for all of them — the observed cost was a paid eval started by a newly added sibling cron, on a schedule nobody asked for, with the bill as the only signal. In a multi-cron file every schedule-gated job must name its cron (`github.event.schedule == '13 5 * * 1'` — a negated `!=` comparison names the cron the job excludes, and an equality against a cron the file never declares is its own finding), every declared cron must be named by at least one job (at-least-once — several jobs may answer one cron, and one job may name several), and a job that runs on every fire — no `if:`, or a vacuous `if: always()` / `if: true` — must carry a reasoned `# multi-cron-ok: <reason>` marker (a placeholder like "n/a" fails). A job gated only by `needs:` inherits its dependencies' gating and is exempt. Single-cron workflows are exempt: the bare event-name gate is unambiguous there.
- New Tier 2 hook `check-path-gate-deps`: verifies every decide-gated job's static dependencies (local composite actions, `.github/scripts/` helpers one `source` hop deep, and `# gate-deps:`-declared paths) are covered by the decide job's path filters, so a PR changing only a dependency can't silently skip the job and green-light its `always()` reporter. Suppress a single dependency with `# path-gate-ok: <dep> <reason>`; a `uses: ./<dir>` naming a missing local action is its own hard error. Registered `always_run` so dependency-side changes (a new file under a covered dir) re-fire the check.
- `check-pending-cancel-concurrency` (Tier 2): flags a per-ref/per-PR
  `concurrency.group` (workflow-level **or** job-level, which
  `check-static-concurrency` never inspects) on a required-check workflow whose
  `on.pull_request.types` includes a type beyond opened/synchronize/reopened.
  Such types (`labeled`, `closed`, …) fire extra runs on the **same head SHA**;
  GitHub's one-running + one-pending slot per group then cancels a current-SHA
  sibling, and its `always()` reporter resolves `cancelled` → the required check
  goes red with no real failure (`cancel-in-progress` only picks which
  current-SHA run dies). Safe fixes: drop the group or key it on
  `github.run_id`; opt out with `# pending-cancel-ok`. Downstream repos guarding
  this with a file-scoped test (e.g. `test_deps_release_scan_event_gating.py`
  covering only `deps-release.yaml`) can retire it in favor of this lint once
  they bump their pin.
- `check-pin-comment-truth` (Tier 2): requires a wellformed `# vX[.Y[.Z]]` comment on every SHA-pinned `uses:` and one consistent comment per `owner/repo@sha` repo-wide (offline; no registry resolution). Opt out with `# pin-comment-ok`.
- `check-provenance-repo-url` (Tier 1, Identity): compares `package.json` `repository.url` and `pyproject.toml` `[project.urls]` repository keys against the local `origin` remote (normalized), and fails a workflow that runs `npm/pnpm publish` with no `repository.url` — the mismatch npm provenance rejects with E422 on a fork's first release.
- `check-replacement-expansion`: a new Extras lint that bans an assembled string in a replacement position. `String.replace`/`replaceAll` and `re.sub`/`re.subn` read the replacement as a pattern before they insert it. JavaScript expands `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$1`; Python expands `\1` and `\g<name>`. A literal stays clean, because the author reads every character of it. A template literal with a hole, an f-string, a concatenation, or a name this file binds to one of those is reported. The remedy is a function replacer, which inserts its return value verbatim. Both languages are read with their own grammar — `_js_ast` and `_py_ast` — so the idiom inside a comment or a string literal is not a finding. Opt out with `allow-replacement-expansion: <reason>`.
- `check-required-reporter` (Tier 2): a gated workflow’s `if: always()` reporter
  jobs must each carry a `# required-check: true|false` classification, so a new
  status check can’t silently ship green-but-never-required. Opt a workflow out
  with `# not-required-check` on its `pull_request:` trigger, or a single reporter
  with `# required-check: false  # <reason>`.
- New Tier 2 hook `check-requires-concurrency`: requires every `pull_request`/`pull_request_target`-triggered workflow to declare a `concurrency:` block, so a new push cancels the superseded run instead of stacking a second full run on a capped runner pool. This closes the gap left by `check-concurrency`, which only validates a block that already exists. The block may sit at the workflow level or on any job (the doctrine-approved shape for a required check that needs serialization). Push-only, schedule-only, and reusable (`workflow_call`) workflows are exempt. Opt out with `# concurrency-not-required` when queue-don't-cancel is intended.
- New Tier 2 hook `check-reusable-permissions`: a job that calls a local reusable workflow with `uses: ./.github/workflows/…` must grant every permission that workflow asks for. GitHub refuses to start a called workflow that requests more than its caller holds. One permission added to a shared workflow therefore stops every caller at once, and the error names the callee, which is correct as written. The check compares the two static `permissions:` blocks. It follows the call one more hop when the middle job declares no block of its own. It also reports a caller that declares no block at all, because the token then carries the repository default, which the workflow file does not state. Suppress one calling job with `# reusable-permissions-ok: <reason>`. A `./` path with no file on disk is its own hard error.
- `check-secret-file-perms` (Extras, picked up automatically by the `check-extras` aggregate): flags a shell line that creates a secret-named file (path matching `token`/`secret`/`cred`/`key`/`passwd`/`password`/`npmrc`/`auth`/`pem`/`refresh`/`cookie`/`id_rsa`) world-readable — via a `>`/`>>` redirect, `touch`, `tee`, or non-private `install` — and only `chmod 0?[46]00`s it private within the next ~3 non-blank lines. That later chmod is the tell that the author knew the file must be private but created it readable first, leaving a window a co-tenant can read. Guarded creates never fire: a standing `umask 0?77` earlier in the file, an inline `(umask 077; …)` on the create line, or `install -m 0?[46]00`. A create with no nearby chmod is not flagged (near-zero false positives). Suppress a deliberate case with `# secret-perms-ok: <reason>` on the create line.
- **`check-soft-timeout`** (Tier 1 · Honesty) — a time limit that the bounded command can ignore. At the deadline, `timeout 60 cmd` sends SIGTERM. A command can catch that signal, block it, or never reach its handler. The command then runs past the limit, and whatever waits on it keeps waiting. Two measured escapes: an `npm` install blocked on a dead registry socket outlived a 180-second limit by 8 minutes 36 seconds; a wedged sandbox held an incident kill switch on its first target while every later target kept running. `--kill-after=N` schedules SIGKILL, which no process can catch, and that makes the limit real. The check reads the bash grammar, so it finds three positions a text search misses or misreads: the command `timeout 60 cmd`, the wrapped call `sbx exec box -- timeout 60 cat /x`, and the array form `run=(timeout 600)` that the shell expands later. A `timeout` inside a message string or a heredoc body is text, and the check ignores it. `-s KILL` passes, because it sends the unstoppable signal first. Opt out with `# allow-soft-timeout: <reason>`.
- `check-stderr-merge-parse` (Tier 2): flags `2>&1`-merged output being parsed — piped into head/tail/grep/awk/cut/sed/jq/sort/wc inside a substitution, or a merged capture later piped/compared — while never flagging diagnostic captures. Scans shell files and workflow inline `run:` blocks. Opt out with `# stderr-merge-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-stray-tool-markup` (Extras): bans stray agent tool-call markup accidentally committed into a file — a line that is entirely a leaked closing/opening tool-call tag (`</invoke>`, an opening `invoke`/`parameter` tag, `<function_calls>`, a bare closing `content` tag, and the `antml:`-prefixed variants). Only whole-line bare tags are flagged; inline mentions, inline-code spans, and fenced code blocks are skipped. Suppress a genuine case with `allow-stray-markup: <reason>` on the line above.
- `check-test-predicate-shadow` (Extras): flags a shell test that redefines a production **pure predicate** — a function whose body only tests and returns. Stubbing a dependency stays legitimate; a predicate has no side effect to intercept, so redefining one substitutes the test's own (usually weaker) copy of the logic and the shipped predicate can regress unseen. Purity is decided on the real bash grammar, so anything richer than a flat `[[ … ]]` / `(( … ))` / `return`/`true`/`false` chain reads as impure and is never flagged. Opt out with `# predicate-shadow-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-tier1` / `check-tier2` / `check-extras` aggregate hooks: enable a whole tier with one id instead of listing each check. A check added to that tier later is picked up with no consumer config change. (`check-absolute-symlinks`, a shell hook, stays separately opt-in.)
- `check-token-fallback` (Tier 2): flags `secrets.A || secrets.B` fallbacks in token positions, where setting the first secret silently switches the workflow's push identity. Opt out with `# token-fallback-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-toolchain-skips` (Extras): flags `pytest.mark.skipif`/`pytest.importorskip` conditions gated on binary discovery (`shutil.which` etc.) with no CI env guard, so a runner missing the tool fails loud instead of silently skipping the guarded coverage. Opt out with `# toolchain-skip-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-trusted-base` (Tier 1, Security): flags the pwn-request shape — a `pull_request(_target)` job that checks out the PR **head** ref _and_ runs privileged (write `permissions:` or a `secrets.*` in `env:`), so the PR author's code executes with the base repo's token and secrets. Read-only, secret-free head checkouts are not flagged; opt out with `# trusted-base-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-uncached-download` (Tier 2): reports a job that downloads a version-pinned tool and holds no cache. The pin makes the bytes identical on every run, so each push to each pull request pays for the same fetch, and a slow registry turns that cost into a job timeout GitHub reports as “cancelled”. Local composite actions are inlined first, so a job that caches through a shared setup action counts as cached. Anything with no stable cache key is left alone: an unpinned install belongs to `check-versionless-install`, and a URL built from the runner's own `$GITHUB_SHA` or `$GITHUB_REF_NAME` names a different object on every run. Opt out with `# cache-exempt: <reason>`.
- `check-unpaged-all` (Extras): it bans an all-shaped verdict over one page of a GitHub listing. GitHub answers a listing under a `total_count` envelope, and one page holds 100 rows, so `all(...)`, `any(...)`, `.every(...)` or `.some(...)` over that page reads a longer listing as a pass. The check fires on a file that reads the GitHub API, names a listing key (`jobs`, `check_runs`, `workflow_runs`, `artifacts`, `check_suites`, `workflows`), reduces a list, and mentions no paging. It reads Python through `ast` and JavaScript or TypeScript through tree-sitter. Opt out with `# allow-unpaged-all: <reason>`.
- New `check-unscoped-tool-grant` (Tier 1, security): flags an unscoped or inert
  file-tool rule in a Claude Code tool grant inside a workflow — `--allowedTools`
  / `--allowed-tools`, an `*ALLOWED_TOOLS` env var, or a legacy `allowed_tools:`
  input. Two classes, both established by probing the real CLI (2.1.220) headless
  against a stub API, every case against a matched denying control:
  - A file tool named with **no path** (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Write`, `Edit`,
    `NotebookEdit`, `MultiEdit`) is a whole-tool grant applied _after_ the
    per-path working-directory check, overriding its verdict — so an `--add-dir`
    beside it is prompt suppression, not a jail. A bare grant is strictly per
    tool name: bare `Read` does not cover `Grep`, bare `Edit` does not cover
    `Write`. Opt out per half with `# allow-unscoped-read-grant: <reason>` /
    `# allow-unscoped-write-grant: <reason>` — legitimate when the same job also
    grants bare `Bash`, since a redirect writes anything regardless.
  - A path rule spelled under any name but `Read` or `Edit` is a rule **nothing
    consults**: `Write(//out.json)` _denies_ the write it appears to grant.
    `Edit(...)` is the spelling that confines Edit, Write, MultiEdit and
    NotebookEdit, and an absolute path needs two leading slashes or the rule
    anchors at the CLI's cwd. This class has **no** opt-out.
    `DISALLOWED_TOOLS` is deliberately excluded, so the lint can never push an
    author to narrow a deny list. The grant scan runs over comment-stripped source,
    so a grant merely quoted in a comment is not linted.
- `check-untrusted-exec` (Tier 1 · Security, default-on, included in `check-tier1`): fails a job that checks out a pull-request head and then executes code resolved from that checkout — a local composite action (`uses: ./…`), a package-manager script (`pnpm <script>` / `npm run …` / `yarn …` / `npx …` / `make …`), or a workspace-relative path (`bash ./scripts/x.sh`) — while any secret is live in the job. Reaches heads `check-trusted-base` cannot see (a matrix-derived `head_ref`, an unpinned `workflow_run` head) and is deliberately NOT silenced by `# trusted-base-ok`, so it audits that opt-out's usual "only runs the trusted base copy" claim. Opt out per job with `# untrusted-exec-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-unused-reusable-input` (Extras): reports a `workflow_call` input that no local caller passes in a `with:` block. Such an input is either dead surface — described, threaded into a step's `env:`, and never set by any run — or the shared answer nobody wired, and the second is what grows a duplicate implementation: a decide gate shipped a `paths-regex-file` input built to read a trigger regex out of a shell file, no workflow passed it, and a sibling workflow needing exactly that grew a 65-line bespoke script with its own copy of the range resolution, the draft skip and the path match. A reusable workflow that no local job calls is skipped, because its callers may live in another repository and this tree cannot see their `with:` blocks. Suppress one input with `# unused-input-ok: <reason>` on its key line or a direct-child line; the reason is mandatory, and a placeholder such as "n/a" fails.
- `check-versionless-install` (Tier 1 · identity): flags an install command that
  names no version — `pip install ruff`, `apt-get install -y pkg`,
  `pipx install pre-commit`, `uv tool install ruff`, `npm install -g pnpm` — in
  shell scripts and inline workflow `run:` blocks, so CI cannot silently install
  different bytes than the ones you reviewed. Requirements/constraints files,
  local paths and archives, URL/VCS specs, variable-built specs, and local (non
  `-g`) npm installs are out of scope; opt out with `# pin-exempt: <reason>`.
- New Extras hook `check-workflow-refs`: fails when a doc or comment cites a GitHub Actions workflow file that no longer exists under `.github/workflows/` — the rot left behind when workflows are consolidated or renamed, invisible to link checkers because the citation is a bare basename (`release-prep.yaml`). Reads only comment bodies and non-fenced prose, resolves against the git-tracked workflow set, and ignores a basename that matches any tracked file or that an ecosystem reserves for something else (`pnpm-lock.yaml`, `compose.yml`, `action.yaml`); a bare basename counts only inside `.github/` or on a line carrying CI vocabulary, while a `.github/workflows/<name>.ya?ml` path always counts. `CHANGELOG.md` and `changelog.d/` are skipped as audit records, and a cross-repo reference is suppressed with `allow-workflow-ref: <reason>`.
- `check-workflow-run-branch-filter` (Extras): reports a `workflow_run` listener with no `branches:` or `branches-ignore:` filter. GitHub creates a run for every completion of every watched workflow, on every branch, and the listener's own `if:` runs after the run exists. A run whose jobs all skip therefore costs the same run-creation path as a real one: about 3,000 such no-op runs sat `in_progress` at once, GitHub stopped dispatching `merge_group` check runs for about 7 hours, and the merge queue merged nothing in that window. Every one of those runs reported success. The check also reports a filter that narrows nothing (`branches: ['**']`, an empty list under either key) and the bare-name spelling `on: [workflow_run]`, which can carry no filter. Opt out with `# unfiltered-listener-ok: <reason>` on the `workflow_run:` key line or a direct-child line; the reason is mandatory, and a placeholder such as "n/a" fails.
- `check-workflow-secret-names` (Tier 2): round-trips every `secrets.*`/`vars.*` name referenced under `.github/` against a checked-in `.github/workflow-secrets.txt` allowlist (both directions, `GITHUB_TOKEN` implicit) and prints the corrected file on mismatch, so a misspelled secret fails at commit time instead of silently degrading at runtime.
- `check-external-clock-targets` (extra): a host outside GitHub can fire a repository's sweeps on a clock it owns. The clock reads a manifest of workflow file names and dispatches each one. The hook fails an entry that names a missing workflow, a workflow with no `workflow_dispatch` trigger, or one with a required default-less input. Each such entry drops every dispatch with no red mark. The default manifest is `.github/scheduler/sweeps.txt`; override it with `--manifest PATH`.
- `check-flag-arity` (Extras, picked up automatically by the `check-extras` aggregate): flags a `case` arm whose label is a value-taking CLI flag (`-x` / `--xxx` / `--xxx=*`) that reads `$2` or does `shift 2` while relying only on the parse loop's outer `[[ $# -gt 0 ]]` — which proves `$1` exists, not `$2`. Passing such a flag last makes `$2` unbound, so under `set -u` the parser dies with a raw `$2: unbound variable` instead of a clean "flag needs a value". Satisfied by an in-arm arity guard (`[[ $# -ge 2 ]] || die`, `(( $# >= 2 ))`, or a negative `-lt 2` bail), a self-guarding read (`${2:?…}` / `${2:-…}`), or a `need_val` / `need_arg` helper; suppress a deliberate case with `# flag-arity-ok: <why>`.
- `check-failure-notifier-coverage` accepts `--notifier-pattern REGEX`
  (repeatable), teaching notifier DISCOVERY a house sink the built-in patterns do
  not name (`--notifier-pattern tell-the-humans`). As in
  `check-cron-alert-coverage`, the flag extends the built-in patterns rather than
  replacing them, so naming a house sink can never silently un-recognize the
  sinks already matched. The two checks now read one shared sink list
  (`_linecheck.NOTIFIER_PATTERNS`), so a sink taught to one is a sink to both.
- `check-pinned-base-images` gained an opt-in `--fix` mode: it resolves each
  unpinned `FROM`'s current registry digest and rewrites the line in place
  (`FROM node:22` → `FROM node:22@sha256:…`), preserving `--platform` flags and
  `AS <stage>` suffixes. `--fix` is the lint's only network path (a Docker
  Registry v2 manifest lookup); detection stays offline. Images whose digest
  can't be resolved are left untouched and still reported.
- `check-pinned-downloads` now also flags a Dockerfile `ADD <url> <dest>` that fetches an `http(s)://` artifact without a nearby checksum/signature check — the idiomatic Dockerfile download was previously invisible to the lint even though it already ran on Dockerfiles. Docker's own `ADD --checksum=sha256:<digest>` counts as the verification, and the existing `# pin-exempt: <reason>` opt-out applies.
- `check-pinned-downloads` now also flags a `# pin-exempt`'d download whose first later use runs it — `bash`/`sh`/`source`/`.`/`chmod +x` on the saved file — with no `[[ -s FILE ]]` (or equivalent) check between the download and the run. An empty file (a 200 response with an empty body, a dead proxy, a full disk) makes `curl -f` report success and the run exit 0 having done nothing, so the install silently reports success and installs nothing. Opt out with `# empty-download-ok: <reason>`.
- New Tier 1 honesty lint `check-pipefail-grep-pipe` bans `producer | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail`. When `grep -q` matches early it closes the pipe and the still-writing producer dies with `SIGPIPE` (exit 141); `pipefail` then surfaces 141 as the pipeline status, so a genuine match is misread as no-match once the producer's output outgrows the ~64 KiB pipe buffer. The lint flags a pipefail-scoped shell file (including sourced `# shellcheck shell=bash` libraries, which inherit strict mode from their callers) that pipes a streaming producer into a quiet grep, and directs authors to the capture-then-here-string fix (`out="$(producer)"; grep -q PAT <<<"$out"`). Bounded builtin producers (`echo`/`printf`/`:`) are exempt; a provably-tiny non-builtin case opts out with `# pipefail-grep-ok: <reason>`.
- Four new Extras lints, all picked up automatically by the `check-extras` aggregate:
  - `check-drift-guards`: a test whose name/docstring reads as a copies-agree "drift guard" must carry `@pytest.mark.drift_guard("<why no SSOT is feasible>")`, so the missing single source of truth is a reviewed judgement, not an implied one.
  <!-- allow-graceful: this bullet documents the lint's own banned word and opt-out token -->
  - `check-graceful-handwave`: bans "graceful"/"gracefully" in prose (Markdown/RST, every line) and code (comments only) as a stand-in for unstated behaviour; opt out by stating it — `allow-graceful: <what actually happens>`; `--prose` scans a free-standing text file (e.g. a PR body) line-by-line.
  - `check-historical-comments`: bans historical narration in code comments ("renamed from", "now uses", "switched to", …) — describe the current code, or opt out with `# allow-history: <reason>`.
  - `check-doc-line-refs`: bans exact line-number citations of source files in Markdown docs (`<file>.<ext>:<N>`, `(L<N>)`, `~L<N>`, …); fenced code blocks and `CHANGELOG.md` are skipped; suppress a load-bearing one with `<!-- allow-line-ref: <reason> -->`.
- `check-ready-for-review` (Tier 1 · Honesty): flags a workflow that gates on the pull request's draft flag and does not list `ready_for_review` in its `pull_request` or `pull_request_target` `types:`. A workflow that skips its jobs while the pull request is a draft has deferred that work, not cancelled it. GitHub reports the pull request leaving draft as the `ready_for_review` activity type, and that type is not in the default set (`opened`, `synchronize`, `reopened`). So the workflow never fires again: the draft run stays the last run, its gated jobs are `skipped`, and GitHub counts a skipped check run as a satisfied required check. The check judges two gate shapes, because a repository can write either. The workflow names `github.event.pull_request.draft` in an `if:`, an `env:` value or a `with:` input. Or a job calls a reusable workflow and passes an input whose NAME carries `draft` — there the gate sits in the callee, so the payload field never appears in the caller at all. On a 50-workflow tree the second shape was 10 of the 18 draft-gated workflows, and a check that read only the payload field would have judged 8 of them. A workflow with no pull request trigger is never judged, so a reusable workflow that holds the gate is silent and its caller is the file reported. Opt out with `# ready-for-review-ok`. Included in the `check-tier1` aggregate.
- `release-canary` console script: asserts the semver-max `v*` git tag and the
  changelog's top dated heading agree; prints the labeled values and exits
  non-zero on mismatch. When a `PKGBUILD` is present its `pkgver=` is folded in
  as an optional AUR marker (`--pkgbuild` overrides the path); a build-time
  `pkgver()`/`$(…)` value that can't be read offline is skipped, never a failure.
  Every marker is read locally, so the tool makes no network request.
- Release machinery ported from `claude-guard`: per-change fragments under
  `changelog.d/`, assembled into `CHANGELOG.md` by `scripts/assemble-changelog.mjs`.
  Labeling a PR `release` triggers a conservative (patch/minor, never major)
  version bump on the PR branch (`release-prep.yaml`); merging it tags `vX.Y.Z`
  and publishes the GitHub Release with that version’s notes (`tag-release.yaml`).
- New Tier 2 hook `check-required-event-closure`: every job that a `# required-check: true` job transitively `needs` must run on every event the check gates (`pull_request`, `pull_request_target`, `merge_group`). GitHub counts a `skipped` check run as a satisfied required check. A needed job whose `if:` shuts it off on a gating event therefore turns the check green there with none of its work done. The live case is a `decide` job that skips in the merge queue while its `always()` reporter reads the empty outputs as a clean skip. The hook parses the `if:` expression and evaluates it with only the event facts bound; every other context is unknown. A fork guard, a `needs.decide.outputs.*` gate, or a status function is therefore unknown and never fires it. On the repository that motivated the hook it flagged the three real defects and nothing else. Opt out per job with `# event-scoped-ok: <reason>`.
- `startup-failure-scan` (apply-side console script, not a pre-commit lint and not in any tier aggregate): names the workflows whose runs failed before any job started. GitHub creates a run for a workflow file it cannot load; the run completes, carries a failure, and holds zero jobs. That shape reaches nobody, because every reporting route needs a job: a notifier that watches through `on.workflow_run` has no job to name, an `if: always()` reporter never runs, and the required check it would have posted waits at `Expected — Waiting` instead of turning red. No static lint can find it either, since the file the Actions loader rejects is the file PyYAML parsed happily. The scan reads the whole window for each workflow, and not the newest page of it, so a breakage that was fixed earlier in the week is still reported. It asks for `status=completed` and classifies each conclusion itself — a `status=failure` listing never returns a `startup_failure` run, so the obvious implementation reports every repo healthy. It excludes `cancelled` and `skipped`, which hold zero jobs in normal operation. Exits non-zero on a finding, `--report-only` to publish without failing, and `--format markdown` for a tracking-issue table. The cost is one request for each 100 completed runs, plus one for each failing run that did not conclude `startup_failure`. The Actions API stops paginating at 1000 items, so one workflow costs at most 10 listings; a workflow busier than that is the one case the scan cannot read in full, and the report names it and marks its count as a floor. This repo runs it every Monday from `.github/workflows/startup-failure-scan.yaml`, which consumers can copy; the job needs only the `actions: read` permission. That workflow is in the notifier's watched list, and `tests/test_startup_failure_scan_wiring.py` pins the wiring, so this script cannot repeat the `release-canary` failure of shipping as an entry point that nothing invokes.
- `check-substitution-exit-swallow` (Tier 1 · Honesty): flags a structured-data producer (`jq`/`yq`) feeding a shell loop through a construct that discards its exit status — `done < <(jq …)` / `mapfile < <(yq …)` (process-substitution stdin redirect) and `jq … | while read` (pipeline). Both report on the redirect/pipe, not on the producer, so a query or data error makes the loop iterate zero times while the function returns success — a fail-open. Producer set is curated to `jq`/`yq` (whose non-zero exit is a genuine fail-closed signal); `grep`/`cat`/`find`/`sed` are excluded. Opt out with a reason-bearing `# allow-substitution-exit: <reason>`. Included in the `check-tier1` aggregate.
- `sync-merge-queue` console script: it holds a repo's merge queue rule at parameters that can still merge. It pins `grouping_strategy` to `ALLGREEN` unless you pass `--allow-headgreen`, and it writes `1` over a `max_entries_to_merge` or `max_entries_to_build` that is zero or absent. A positive size is a human's tuning and survives. The script reports three states it must not repair, and exits non-zero on each: a ruleset that is not enforced, a queue whose `merge_method` the repo forbids, and a ruleset with no always-on bypass for the merge queue app. Each state stops every merge while nothing turns red. `--skip-bypass-check` drops the last of the three. `--check` reports the drift and writes nothing. A repo whose branch ruleset carries no merge queue rule exits 0.
- `sync-required-checks` console script (the apply half of
  `check-required-reporter`): derives the required-check set from every job
  carrying `# required-check: true` — expanding each `name:` across its
  `strategy.matrix` — and rewrites the repo's single branch ruleset's
  `required_status_checks` to exactly that set. `--check` reports drift and exits
  non-zero without mutating; the default applies. Reads the marker via the same
  scoping the lint uses, so the two can never disagree.

### Changed

- **BREAKING**: the symlink hook id is now `check-absolute-symlinks`. It was `check-symlinks`. Rename the `- id:` line in your config to keep the hook enabled. The old id was the same string as the `check-symlinks` hook in `pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks`. The two hooks ask different questions. The upstream one rejects a symlink whose target does not exist. This one rejects a symlink whose target is an absolute path. A repo that enabled both ran two hooks under one id, so `pre-commit run check-symlinks` could not select one of them. The packaged script moves with the id, from `ci_truth_serum/check_symlinks.sh` to `ci_truth_serum/check_absolute_symlinks.sh`.
- Every opt-out/annotation token is now matched by one shared comment-scoped
  matcher: the token must sit inside a real comment (`#`, `<!-- -->`, `//`)
  and — for every hook whose contract documents `<token>: <reason>` — carry a
  non-empty reason. A token smuggled into live data (a `group: "<token>"`
  string value, a printed message) no longer silently disables a lint, and a
  bare reason-less marker no longer suppresses hooks that demand a stated
  reason.
- `check-pinned-downloads` recognizes an output flag inside a short-flag
  cluster: `wget -qO- url | jq` is a stdout API read (previously flagged as an
  unverified artifact download), while `wget -qO file` / `curl -fsSLO` remain
  artifacts and `wget -qO- url | sh` still fires; a shell redirect to a file
  now wins over a stdout sink flag (`wget -qO- url > tool` is an artifact).
- `check-drift-guards`' non-Python phrase pass only scans TEST files
  (`tests/`-like directories, `test_*`, `*.test.*`/`*.spec.*`) — production
  scripts' own "keeps X in sync" comments no longer false-positive.
- `check-flag-arity` tracks the arity a guard actually PROVES as a number: a
  `[[ $# -ge 2 ]] || die` no longer clears an arm that reads `$3`/`shift 3`,
  a defaulting `${2:-x}` read no longer excuses a following `shift 2`, and a
  `shift N` lowers the proven bound. Abort-helper names are resolved against
  the file: a locally defined `fail() { echo oops; }` that does not exit no
  longer counts as a bailing guard (undefined conventional names are still
  trusted).
- `check-static-concurrency` / `check-cancellable-required-check`: a per-ref
  concurrency key counts only INSIDE a `${{ … }}` expression — a group string
  merely containing the literal text `github.ref` is static.
- An opt-out annotation may now sit anywhere in the comment block directly above the construct it excuses, and anywhere inside that construct's own source span. The window used to be one line, so a reason that wrapped onto a second line pushed the token out of range and the check still fired. An author who explained WHY was told to reformat. Both `check-toolchain-skips` and `check-case-default` accept the wider window; the block must be unbroken, so a blank line still ends it and an annotation written for something else cannot drift down onto a later construct. The prose checks (`check-graceful-handwave`, `check-historical-comments`, `check-drift-guards`) keep their one-line window: there the flagged line is itself a comment, and one annotation at the top of a paragraph would blanket every later sentence in it. <!-- allow-graceful: names the lint whose banned word this is; it makes no claim about behaviour -->
- Every check now asks one function where an opt-out annotation may sit. `_linecheck.annotation_window` is that function: it accepts the construct's own span plus the unbroken comment block directly above it. The pack previously held about twenty open-coded answers — some accepted the line above, some a whole logical line, some only the flagged line — so the same annotation was honoured by one check and rejected by its neighbour, and an author could not learn the rule once. A wrapped reason now counts everywhere, because prose wraps and the token line moves with it. The window stays bounded: the token must sit in a real comment, it must carry a reason, and the block stops at the first line that is not a comment, so a blank line ends it and an annotation written about something else cannot drift onto a later construct. A contract test bans reaching for a neighbouring line by hand, so the twenty answers cannot grow back.
- This repo's own CI now pins the version it installs: the pre-commit workflow
  installs from `.github/requirements-ci.txt` (a file Dependabot's `pip`
  ecosystem can bump, unlike a version written inline in a `run:` line), and
  `setup.sh` bootstraps pnpm at the version `package.json`'s `packageManager`
  field already declares.
- `check-drift-guards` now also catches drift guards by their **copies-agree structure**, not just intent phrasing: a test that reads an external source and asserts a hand-maintained collection (an in-source literal or an `UPPER_CASE` constant / its `.keys()`) equals it is flagged even when it avoids words like "drift guard" (the laundering case — e.g. a test relabeled an "SSOT-coverage contract"). The trigger is deliberately narrow (0 false positives on this repo's own suite) and skips ordinary output-vs-expected assertions; clear a genuine non-guard with a `# not-a-drift-guard: <reason>` comment.
- `check-frozen-head-sha` now follows an `env:` variable bound to the frozen head SHA, which it previously did not read at all. It reports only where a step SPENDS that variable in a way the frozen value breaks: as an endpoint of a `git` revision range (`git diff $HEAD_SHA...HEAD`), or as `actions/checkout`'s `ref:`. Those are the two positions the direct rule already banned, so an environment variable is no longer a one-hop route around the check. The binding alone stays clean on purpose: routing an expression through `env:` is the shape the template-injection checks want, and on a 50-workflow tree 41 of the 45 uses of the frozen SHA sat under `env:` with no defect among them. Reading a range endpoint is a question about shell structure, so the `run:` script is parsed with the bash grammar and only a `git` command's own words are judged. A range quoted inside a message that a command prints, or written into a heredoc body, names no `git` command and stays silent. The hook now needs `tree-sitter` and `tree-sitter-bash`, which the aggregates already install.
`check-exit-suppression` no longer excuses a suppressed **mutating** git command just because it discards its output. For `git merge`/`commit`/`add`/`reset`/… the "nothing left to surface" reasoning inverts: the stdout is noise, but the exit status is the only evidence the mutation ran, and the next command reads the tree it was supposed to produce — so the failure becomes a wrong answer rather than a silence. Read-only verbs (`grep`, `log`, `rev-parse`, `fetch`, `status`) keep the allowance, and any site can opt out with `# allow-exit-suppress: <reason>`.
- `check-drift-guards`: added a third trigger for the LAUNDERED form — a comment
  that claims a value is authoritative (`SSOT`, `canonical`, `single source of
truth`) while admitting it is a copy (`mirrored from`, `restated here`,
  `hand-maintained`). Neither half fires alone, and a denial governing the copy
  word (`read from the SSOT, never a copy`) suppresses. Closes the gap where a
  copy relabelled as a source of truth used none of the drift vocabulary and so
  read as the sanctioned single-source pattern. Runs on Python tests and on
  JS/TS/shell suites; clear a false positive with `drift-guard-ok: <reason>`.
- `check-drift-guards`: comments are now located by a grammar rather than a text
  scan — Python's `tokenize` for `.py`, tree-sitter-bash for shell. A `#` inside
  a Python string literal, a shell heredoc body, or a quoted shell word is no
  longer read as a comment. This removes three defects: a lint fixture or error
  message quoting the flagged shape no longer false-positives, a heredoc body
  no longer reads as a run of comments (the probe in
  `.claude/rules/shell-lint-parsing.md`), and — the fail-open — a string literal
  spelling `# not-a-drift-guard:` no longer disarms the structural trigger for
  the whole test. JS/TS still uses the text heuristic; no JS grammar is a
  dependency yet.
- Docs: this package is not published to npm or PyPI — its release _is_ the `v*`
  tag consumers pin with pre-commit's `rev:`. The `sync-required-checks` and
  `release-canary` sections now install from that tag
  (`pip install "git+https://github.com/AlexanderMattTurner/ci-truth-serum@v1.0.0"`)
  instead of a registry name that resolves nowhere, and `package.json` is marked
  `private` so a stray `npm publish` cannot invent a registry copy.
- **Breaking:** `check-failure-notifier-coverage` now FAILS CLOSED when no
  notifier workflow can be discovered, where it used to report success. A pass
  from a check that found nothing to check is the vacuous green this package
  exists to catch — and "found nothing" is precisely how a notifier that was
  deleted, renamed, or never synced from the template goes unnoticed. The
  `--require-notifier` flag is replaced (not aliased) by its inverse,
  `--allow-no-notifier`, for a repo that deliberately routes failures nowhere;
  `--notifier FILENAME` (default `ci-failure-notify.yaml`, the shared template's
  spelling) states the filename the fail-closed message should name. The message
  distinguishes "that file is not there" from "that file is there but observes
  nothing" — the second being an inert notifier that reads as coverage in review.
- `notify-ntfy`: each path that notifies nobody now writes a `::warning::` annotation, which GitHub shows on the run summary. There are two such paths, and both stay non-fatal for the reasons they always had: an unset `GH_NTFY_SUBJECT` secret must not redden a repo that never opted in, and a dead ntfy server must not add a second red to a workflow that already failed. The cost of that choice was that a green notifier run proved nothing — the alert may have reached a phone, or the topic may have been empty all year, and the run looked the same either way. The annotation separates the two without changing any exit status. The topic stays out of the output; the annotation names the server and the `curl` exit code only.
- `check-pending-cancel-concurrency` now reads a workflow that declares a required check with a `# required-check: true` marker alone. Before this change the check read only the decide-gate plus `always()`-reporter shape, so a marker-only workflow passed while it carried the exact hazard. On the marker route the check reads the workflow-level `concurrency:` block plus the marked jobs only: an advisory job in a marked workflow reddens no required check.
`check-pipefail-grep-pipe` now finds three shapes of the SIGPIPE misread that it used to miss, and it over-fires less on the shapes it already found.

- A bounded producer must carry only LITERAL arguments. `printf '%s' "$input" | grep -q …` writes as many bytes as `$input` holds, so it can outrun the pipe buffer. Only `echo hello`-style producers keep the exemption.
- A heredoc body whose first line is a shell shebang is parsed as shell. A script that writes a hook out of `<<'HOOK'` emits shell that later runs, and the check now reads it. Hits point at the enclosing file's line numbers. The descent goes one level.
- The reader set is no longer `grep -q` alone. It adds `grep -m N`, `grep -l`, the `egrep`/`fgrep`/`rg` spellings, `head` without a negative count, and `sed` whose script carries a `q`/`Q` quit command.
- The check now needs the pipeline's exit status to be READ: the condition of an `if`/`while`/`until`/`elif`, an operand of `&&`/`||`, or under `!`. A trailing `|| true` discards the status, so nothing can misread it. This gate is what keeps the wider reader set precise.
- **BREAKING**: the installed Python package is now `ci_truth_serum` (was the
  generic top-level name `hooks`, which any consumer repo with its own `hooks/`
  directory on `sys.path` could shadow, breaking every hook). Hook ids are
  unchanged — consumers only bump `rev:`; anything importing the package or
  running `python -m hooks.check_*` directly must switch to
  `python -m ci_truth_serum.check_*`.
- The `README.md` is rewritten in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Every sentence now states one idea and stays within 25 words, in the active voice with an explicit subject. The metaphors are gone: a check no longer "burns" a runner, "rides" a tier, or "pages" a person, and each row says what breaks and for whom. Two shipped checks that the README never documented now have rows: `check-frozen-head-sha` (Tier 1, honesty) and `check-cancellable-required-check` (Tier 2, opinionated). The example config block also lists every Tier 1 hook, so a consumer who copies it enables the whole default-on set rather than a subset. No check behaviour changes.
- `check-failure-notifier-coverage` and `check-cron-alert-coverage` now answer
  "is this workflow's failure routed to a human?" from ONE shared predicate,
  instead of computing overlapping and mutually inconsistent obligations. A
  failure is routed when the workflow self-notifies on the failure path, when a
  discovered notifier lists it in `on.workflow_run.workflows`, when a
  `pull_request` trigger puts its red on a PR, or when it carries a reasoned
  `# cron-alert: false` marker.
- **Behaviour change:** `check-failure-notifier-coverage` no longer demands that
  the notifier list EVERY push/schedule workflow — only the residual whose
  failures reach nobody else. Forcing in an opted-out workflow silently undid the
  sibling lint's sanctioned marker, a self-notifying workflow got paged twice, and
  a workflow whose failure is already a check on the PR paged for a red a reviewer
  was looking at. A repo may still watch more than that minimum: a listed name is
  reported stale only when it matches no workflow in the tree.
- **Behaviour change:** `check-cron-alert-coverage` now accepts a
  failure notifier that watches the scheduled workflow as coverage, so a repo whose
  crons are covered centrally is no longer told to add a notification step that
  would page twice. A `pull_request` trigger is deliberately NOT accepted there: a
  cron fire has no pull request. The `# cron-alert: false` marker is also read from
  the `push:` key, so a push-only workflow can state the same decision.
- Shell lints now read a braced `${VAR}` argument the same way they already read
  `$VAR` and `"$VAR"`. The set of `command` children counted as arguments lived in
  seven separate copies, six of which omitted the `expansion` node type — so in
  those lints the braced spelling alone vanished from the argument list. Two
  verdicts change as a result, both toward agreement with the other two spellings:
  `pip install --target ${D} ruff` is now reported by `check-versionless-install`
  (the flag consumes `${D}`, leaving `ruff` unpinned) and
  `docker ${SUB} build . 2>/dev/null` is no longer reported by
  `check-stderr-suppression` (an opaque word blocks its subcommand scan, as it
  already did for `$SUB`).
- `check-unscoped-tool-grant` reads its opt-out annotation from the same window
  every other check uses: the grant line plus the unbroken comment block above
  it. One grant can trip both the read and the write class, and only one
  annotation fits the single line the check accepted before, so such a grant had
  no way to opt out of both at once.
- `check-versionless-install` now analyses the real bash grammar (tree-sitter)
  instead of scanning text, which removes a class of false positive rather than
  another instance of it: a redirection (`>&2`) is a `file_redirect` and never a
  package spec, a quoted message is a `string` argument of the command that
  prints it, a heredoc body is a heredoc, `&&`/`;`/`|` genuinely separate
  commands, and a `$VAR` spec is an expansion node. An install inside a string is
  judged only where something executes that string (`bash -c`, `eval`, `ssh`,
  `xargs … sh -c`), which is parsed as its own script.
- **Behavior change:** a finding is reported at the line of the install command
  itself, not at the start of the backslash-joined block containing it — so
  `apt-get update && \` on one line and `apt-get install …` on the next is
  reported at the install. A `# pin-exempt:` annotation must therefore sit on (or
  directly above) the install command, which is where it belongs.

### Removed

- `check-cron-staleness-optout` is removed. It asked the right question — a cron
  GitHub disabled for repo dormancy produces no failure, so its silence reads as
  health — but it could not answer it: detecting a stopped schedule needs a
  runtime Actions API query, which a pre-commit pack cannot ship. What was left
  was marker bookkeeping plus an existence check on a watchdog workflow, and the
  watchdog is itself a cron, so repo dormancy disables the watcher along with
  everything it watches. The check was structurally blind in the exact case that
  motivated it. A freshness probe on the PR path is the shape that works: it runs
  when a human is already looking, dormancy cannot disable it, and it needs
  neither a marker discipline nor a watchdog registry. `# cron-stale: false`
  markers are no longer read by anything and can be deleted.
- **Breaking:** `release-canary` no longer reads the npm registry. Its markers
  are the `v*` git tag, the changelog's top dated heading, and an optional
  `PKGBUILD` `pkgver=`, all read locally — the tool now makes no network request
  and needs no registry credentials, so it runs in the same restricted job that
  cut the release. The `--package` flag is gone with the npm marker (no
  `package.json` is read), and so is the `--no-npm` flag added in this same
  release, which existed only to switch the npm marker off.

### Fixed

- `check-always-reporter`, `check-static-concurrency`, and `check-required-reporter` now recognize a `${{ always() }}`-wrapped reporter `if:` as equivalent to bare `always()`. Previously the exact-string match missed the wrapper, so a gated workflow whose reporter used `if: ${{ always() }}` escaped all three checks (false negative). A compound `always() && <cond>` is still intentionally not a reporter.
- Every shell lint that decided on text now decides on the bash grammar:
  `check-exit-suppression`, `check-echo-fallback`, `check-stderr-merge-parse`,
  `check-pinned-downloads` and `check-gh-slurp-jq`. Each stops reporting its own
  banned idiom when it appears in a printed message or a heredoc body — text no
  shell executes — and each removes further structural false positives listed in
  its commit: a quoted `;` splitting a command that was never split, a redirect
  belonging to a different command, a URL path segment read as a command name, a
  redirection read as a flag. Two false NEGATIVES are fixed too: a redirect
  spelled inside a string counted as a real output discard, and a git mutation
  named inside a string revoked an allowance it should not have.
- `check-gh-slurp-jq` now scans inline workflow `run:` blocks. `run_tier` already
  classified it `SHELL_OR_WORKFLOW_YAML`, but its `main()` read a workflow YAML as
  though it were one shell file, so the routing was declared and never ran.
- **Behavior change:** `echo x || true` is now reported by
  `check-exit-suppression`. Its previous excuse list for printing commands was the
  false-positive mechanism, and a suppression on a printing command is still a
  suppression; annotate with `# allow-exit-suppress: <reason>` where it is
  deliberate.
- The shared `tree-sitter-bash` wrapper now folds every supplementary-plane (non-BMP, codepoint ≥ U+10000) character to U+FFFD before parsing. tree-sitter-bash 0.25's C scanner corrupts its heap on such a character next to a word-opening token (e.g. a `{` immediately followed by an astral char), segfaulting the whole process non-deterministically — so `check-case-default`, `check-workflow-pipefail`, and `check-flag-arity` could crash a pre-commit run (or a pytest worker) on hostile or generated input. Folding the char class out up front keeps every shell lint total; a supplementary-plane char is a plain word byte to bash, so the substitution never changes a lint's verdict.
- `check-workflow-pipefail` and `check-flag-arity` now parse shell with a real bash grammar (`tree-sitter-bash`) instead of hand-rolled quote/heredoc/case tokenizers, closing the blind spots those approximations had. `check-workflow-pipefail` now sees a masking pipe that an escaped quote (`echo "a\"" | tee`), a `$'…'` ANSI-C string, or nested `$()`/backtick command substitution previously hid from its char-by-char quote counter. `check-flag-arity` no longer loses a violation when a `;;` or `case … in` appears inside a string, and it excludes reads in nested `case` arms by construction. Both lints gain `tree-sitter` / `tree-sitter-bash` as runtime dependencies (declared in each hook's `additional_dependencies`).
- `scripts/assemble-changelog.mjs` inserts the assembled release section with a function replacer. `String.prototype.replace` expands `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$1` in a replacement string. A changelog fragment holds arbitrary prose, so it can contain any of them. In `$'`, the pattern means "the text after the match". One fragment quoted a shell `$'…'` string, and the assembler copied the whole rest of `CHANGELOG.md` into the middle of the new section. That broke the v1.1.0 cut: the release PR duplicated the `## [1.0.0]` block inside its own `### Fixed` list, and the split bullet failed `markdownlint` MD038.
- The gitleaks download is now checksum-verified against a committed SHA-256 before execution, and post-merge tagging detects a version advance against the latest release tag so releases are no longer silently skipped under rebase-and-merge.
- `check-workflow-secret-names`, `check-token-fallback` and
  `check-provenance-repo-url` no longer read a YAML `#` comment as workflow
  content. A comment merely _mentioning_ `secrets.NAME`, the
  `secrets.A || secrets.B` idiom, or `npm publish` used to produce a finding
  whose only remedy was to pad `.github/workflow-secrets.txt` (or
  `package.json`) with something the workflows never use — weakening the very
  allowlist that catches a misspelled secret. Comment detection now defers to
  PyYAML's scanner, so a `#` inside a quoted scalar (`title: "#general"`) or a
  `run:` block scalar stays content and a real reference after it on the same
  line is still checked.
- A check can no longer report a clean pass over files it never scanned. This had two shapes. A check that scans the paths you name looped zero times over an empty argument list and returned 0 — the exit code of a real pass — so a caller who forgot the file list read it as "this repository is clean". All 27 such checks now share one entry point, `run_file_cli`, which refuses an empty run with exit 2 and prints the command that scans the whole tree. A check that finds its own files under `.github/` returned 0 in silence when it found none; exit 0 is honest there, because a repository with no workflow has none to violate, so those say on standard error that they scanned nothing. `check-provenance-repo-url` says the same when the repository has no `origin` remote to compare against, and the shell checks that read the whole tracked tree say it when the tree holds no shell file.
- The workflow checks share one file-discovery definition again. Nine of them carried a private copy that read the same two globs, and each copy was a place the notice above could go missing. `workflow_files` now takes the composite-action directory as an optional argument, which is the only way the copies differed.
- Closed three fail-open decide-filter gaps the new `check-path-gate-deps` hook found in this repo's own workflows: `lint.yaml` and `node-tests.yaml` omitted `.github/scripts/script-configured.sh`, and `validate-config.yaml` omitted `.github/scripts/validate-config.sh` — a PR changing only those scripts skipped the gated jobs while their reporters stayed green.
- `check-exit-suppression` no longer false-positives on a `|| true` inside a `$( … )` / `<( … )` value capture that spans multiple lines (the multi-line form of the already-allowed single-line `var=$(cmd || true)`). It also no longer miscounts an escaped backtick (`\``) when deciding whether a suppressor sits inside a capture.
- The four comment-reading lints now locate comments in JavaScript/TypeScript
  with a real grammar (tree-sitter-javascript / tree-sitter-typescript) instead
  of scanning for a `//` delimiter, closing the last language for which "is this
  a comment?" was answered by the text. Measured over 241 real `.mjs`/`.js`/`.ts`
  files: 169 lines the delimiter scan called comments are not (a `#!` hashbang, a
  `**bold**` line inside a template literal read as a `/* … */` continuation),
  and 250 real comment lines it missed (an inline `/** @type {…} */` cast, a
  block comment's opening and closing lines). A `.ts` file is parsed by the
  TypeScript grammar and a `.tsx` by its own, since under the wrong one a type
  annotation is a syntax error that drops every comment after it.
  The four: `check-drift-guards`, `check-historical-comments`,
  `check-workflow-refs`, `check-graceful-handwave`. <!-- allow-graceful: names the lint whose banned word this is; it makes no claim about behaviour -->
- The same lints now number physical lines by `\n`, matching the line numbering
  every grammar reports. `str.splitlines()` also breaks on `\v`, `\f`, `\x85` and
  U+2028/U+2029, so a file containing one of those had every later reported line
  number off by the difference.
- Three of those hooks declared **no** `additional_dependencies` while already
  importing PyYAML through `_linecheck` — latent until a downstream repo enabled
  one of the ids directly rather than through the `check-extras` aggregate. All
  now declare PyYAML plus the grammar bindings.
- New shared module `ci_truth_serum/_comments.py` is the one place a lint asks
  which lines carry narration: `tokenize` for Python, tree-sitter-bash for shell,
  tree-sitter-{javascript,typescript} for JS/TS, and a documented delimiter scan
  only for a language with no grammar here (YAML). The four lints previously
  routed this three different ways.
- README: the “What it checks” tables rendered wrong. Three rows
  (`check-folded-scalar-comment`, `check-gh-slurp-jq`,
  `check-unscoped-tool-grant`) sat one blank line below their table, which ends
  a GFM table — they shipped as stray lines of literal `| pipe | text |`. Two
  more cells carried unescaped `|` characters that split them into phantom
  columns, truncating the visible text and mangling `check-trusted-base`’s
  wording. All are fixed, and markdownlint now runs over every `.md` file (in
  `pnpm lint`, pre-commit, and CI) with a local `orphan-table-row` rule that
  reports a severed table row — the one no stock rule sees, because the parser
  never accepted it as a table row to begin with.
- The mutation shards for `_linecheck.py` no longer run out of time. A module's mutation oracle is its own test file, re-run once for every mutant, so a test that spawns 50 subprocesses costs 50 spawns per mutant. The two registry-wide contract tests that do this now live in `tests/cts/test_empty_scan_contract.py`, which is nobody's oracle. The shard budget is unchanged.
- `check-failure-notifier-coverage` no longer goes blind in a repo whose notifier
  workflow is not literally named `ci-failure-notify.yaml`. It matched that one
  basename and nothing else, so a repo calling its notifier anything else
  (`build-publish-notify.yaml`, `alerts.yaml`) got a green from a check that had
  found nothing and verified nothing, and the old `--require-notifier` reported
  the notifier "missing" while it sat in the same directory. That filename is
  still the expected default (it is the shared template's spelling), but it is
  now only the name the fail-closed message states — never a filter. The notifier
  is DISCOVERED: a
  workflow qualifies when it is triggered `on.workflow_run` **and** names a
  notification sink (in its own `name:`, a job's `name:`/`uses:`, or a step's
  `uses:`/`name:`/`run:`). Both halves are required — the trigger alone would
  mistake any CI workflow with a Slack step for the notifier, the sink alone
  would hold an unrelated `workflow_run` consumer to the notifier's
  exhaustiveness invariant. More than one notifier is allowed: coverage is the
  union of their lists, while a stale or duplicated entry is still reported
  against the file that carries it.
- `check-cron-alert-coverage` recognizes an issue-management step as the failure
  sink it is. The pattern was `create[-_]issue`, so a repo that routes failures
  through a house script (`manage-release-failure-issue.sh open`) or a step named
  "Open a tracking issue if the run failed" was reported as routing its failures
  nowhere — a false positive that pushes a repo toward a bogus opt-out marker for
  coverage it actually has. Any issue-management verb (`create`/`open`/`file`/
  `manage`/`report`) preceding `issue`/`issues` now counts; a step that merely
  mentions issues without such a verb (`gh issue list --state open`) still does
  not.
- The last five lints that decided on text now decide on a grammar. The three
  remaining shell lints — `check-substitution-exit-swallow`,
  `check-stderr-suppression` and `check-secret-file-perms` — read the bash
  grammar (`_bash_ast`), and the two Python lints — `check-global-stdio-swap` and
  `check-toolchain-skips` — read Python's own (`ast`, via the new `_py_ast`; no
  new dependency). Every structural question each was approximating is now
  answered by a node: which stages a pipeline holds, which command a redirect
  belongs to and in what ORDER bash applies it, whether a token is a subcommand
  or a flag's value, which statements follow a create, whether a name is an
  assignment target, and where a call's argument list ends.
- The two Python lints stop flagging their own docstrings, test fixtures and any
  other idiom spelled inside a string literal — 23 findings on this repo's own
  tree, every one a false positive, which is why both had been muted in
  `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. `check-toolchain-skips` is un-muted over the fixture
  files it used to flag; `check-global-stdio-swap` stays skipped for its
  documented scoping reason alone.
- False NEGATIVES fixed: a launch or a `jq`/`yq` producer written after a logging
  call on the same line is now judged (the old scan excused the whole line
  because its first word printed something); a launcher reached through `sudo`,
  an absolute path, or a group redirect (`{ docker build .; } >/dev/null 2>&1`)
  is now seen; a stream bound by `with … as sys.stdout`, across lines, or through
  `setattr(sys, "stdout", …)` is now a swap; and a `skipif` whose `reason=` merely
  mentions `CI` no longer passes as CI-guarded.
- **Behavior change:** `2>&1 >/dev/null` is no longer reported by
  `check-stderr-suppression`. Bash applies redirects left to right, so that order
  dups stderr onto the still-live stdout and then moves only stdout — stderr
  survives, and nothing is suppressed. `>/dev/null 2>&1` still is.
- `check-pinned-base-images --fix` now inserts a resolved digest with a function replacer. The digest is text a remote registry sent, and `re.sub` expands `\1` and `\g<name>` in a replacement string, so a hostile digest could rewrite the `FROM` line it pins.
- `check-pinned-downloads` no longer reports a command because a LATER `&&`
  branch redirects to a file. tree-sitter wraps `a && b > f` in one
  `redirected_statement` around the whole list, but bash gives `> f` to `b`
  alone; crediting every branch made an `apt-get install … curl …` look like a
  fetch that saved a file, and the bogus finding then squeezed the real download
  beside it out of its own verification window. A `{ …; } > f` / `( …; ) > f`
  group still covers every command inside it.
- `check-pipefail-grep-pipe` now parses scripts with tree-sitter-bash instead of
  scanning physical lines, closing two evasions: a pipeline wrapped across lines
  (trailing `|` / backslash continuations) is analyzed as one pipeline, and a
  `set -o pipefail` appearing only AFTER the pipeline (or in dead code) no longer
  arms — or excuses — the wrong pipes: the first pipefail-enabling command must
  precede the pipeline in source order (function bodies are gated on pipefail
  anywhere in the file, since they run at call time). A `|` inside a string,
  comment, or heredoc is never mistaken for a pipe.
- `check-test-predicate-shadow` no longer reports clean on the commit that lands the shadow from the production side. A violation is a pair — a test-side definition and a production-side pure predicate — so scanning only the files pre-commit passes missed the case where the production half is what changed: making a shipped function a pure predicate, or renaming one onto a name a long-untouched test file already defines, created the pair with no test file in the file list. The passed list now only ever narrows the scan (a production file in it widens the test side to the whole tree), so the empty-baseline guarantee the check is worth anything for holds on every commit, not only on test-side ones.
- `release-canary` no longer crashes with an `npm view` traceback when a package
  is absent from the registry — it no longer talks to npm at all (see the
  Removed entry).
- Release automation no longer stops when one model credential is exhausted: `release-readiness.sh` and `release-prep.sh` now walk a five-rung credential ladder (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and its three fallbacks, all passed through the workflows' `env:`), skipping unset rungs and treating an HTTP 400/401/403 as terminal for that credential only instead of fatal for the run. Neither script requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` up front any more, and when every rung is missing or rejected `release-readiness.sh` derives the bump from the pending `changelog.d/` fragment categories and still opens the release PR — announcing the degradation in the log, the job summary, and the PR body rather than reporting a verdict nobody made.
- The tier aggregates (`check-tier1` / `check-tier2` / `check-extras`) now name the checks that had no file to scan. A content lint reads only the files it is given, so a commit that touches one language leaves the other content lints with nothing to do — and they exited 0, the same code as a pass. A hand run with no file arguments hit the worst form: every workflow lint ran, no content lint did, and the run reported a clean tier. The note goes to stderr and lists each check by name. When the caller passed no files at all, it also gives the command that scans the whole tree.
- All line-oriented shell lints (`check-stderr-suppression`,
  `check-substitution-exit-swallow`, `check-pinned-downloads`,
  `check-secret-file-perms`, plus the joiners `check-exit-suppression`,
  `check-echo-fallback`, `check-stderr-merge-parse` already had privately) now
  scan through ONE shared logical-line joiner, so a construct wrapped across
  physical lines (trailing `|`/`\` continuations, multi-line `$(…)` captures)
  can no longer evade any of them.
- `check-case-default` now finds `case` blocks with tree-sitter-bash: a
  single-line `case … esac` (previously never checked — the hand-rolled stack
  scanner leaked its frame on the same-line `esac`) is analyzed like any other
  block, and a `case` quoted in a string or comment is never mistaken for one.
- `check-flag-arity` parses through the same shared `_bash_ast` grammar module
  as the other AST lints.
- Shell-pattern hooks now catch equivalent banned idioms that previously slipped past: `check-stderr-suppression` flags the canonical `>/dev/null 2>&1`; `check-pinned-downloads` flags a bare `wget <url>` (saved to disk by default) and a `curl … > FILE` / `>> FILE` redirect; `check-workflow-pipefail` drops quoted-heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) bodies so a pipe outside is still seen and a `|` inside isn't a false positive, and only honors an `# allow-no-pipefail` opt-out in a real comment (not in a string or heredoc body); `check-unnamed-regex-groups` resolves `import re as x` / `from re import compile` aliases; `check-exit-suppression` catches `|| true` glued to a following metacharacter (`|| true&`).
- Restored the repo-local behaviour that the template sync overwrote: the ntfy
  notifier again writes a `::warning::` annotation on each path that notifies
  nobody, the phone-home workflow again reads one `$PHONE_HOME_DIR` and installs
  gitleaks through the checksum-verifying installer, and `release-canary.sh` again
  runs this package's own `release-canary` console script.
- `decide-pr-review-trigger.sh` no longer passes `--slurp` and `--jq` to one
  `gh api` call. `gh` rejects that pair while parsing its arguments, so the call
  exited 1 before any request and the `|| true` swallowed it — every push read as
  "no reviewer hold" and the automatic re-review never fired.
- `check-drift-guards` and `check-toolchain-skips` no longer skip the shortest
  test-file names. Each hand-rolled its own "is this a test file?" path filter and
  both were silently DEAD for `test.py`, `x/test.py` and `conftest.py` (and
  drift-guards also for `spec.rb`, `x/spec.js`, `specs/`), because the bare-basename
  alternative demanded a separator after `test`. A `skipif` hiding in `conftest.py`
  — where collection-time skips most naturally live — escaped `check-toolchain-skips`
  entirely. A scope filter's recall bug is invisible: it produces a green vacuous
  pass, never an error. There is now one shared predicate rather than two peers to
  drift, and a guard test asserts nothing else re-derives it.
- `check-claude-model`'s `uses:` matcher put the optional `-` before the indent
  run (`^-?\s*uses:`), so it matched an indented block-sequence entry only because
  its caller pre-stripped the line. Corrected to `^\s*-?\s*` and the strip dropped,
  so the pattern is right on its own. A commented-out or example `# uses: …` line
  still never matches.
- A shell file the bash grammar cannot read no longer reports clean. tree-sitter does not raise on malformed input — it recovers into error nodes and continues — and that recovery is not local in effect: one construct it cannot read drops the nodes a detector matches on for the rest of the file. Every grammar-based check therefore returned an empty result for a file it never really read, which is the same result it returns for a file it read and found clean. Measured with `check-exit-suppression`: a single `${x%%]*}` on line 2 hid a `|| true` on line 3 that the same check reports on line 3 of an otherwise identical file. The whole-file path now refuses such a file by name and line, and names the rewrite. `parse` itself stays permissive, because the workflow checks legitimately hand it `run:` blocks that carry `${{ … }}` — GitHub Actions syntax, not bash.
- `UnparseableShellError` now names a byte offset and one remedy. It already named a line number. Fix the syntax using the known triggers listed in the class docstring.
